The NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 has a release date of April 13, 2023 and an MSRP of $600. We're reviewing the video card today, testing the RTX 4070 GPU with the NVIDIA Founders Edition model. One of the key comparisons currently -- maybe surprisingly -- is actually AMD's RX 6950 XT, which has plummeted in price over the last year or two. We're also benchmarking the RTX 4070 vs. the RTX 3070, RTX 2070, and GTX 1070, giving 4 generations of the 70-class. Of course, other test data includes the RTX 4090, 4080, and 4070 Ti vs. the RTX 4070, with comparisons to plenty of 30-series and 6000-series cards. Although the 7900 XT and XTX are in the charts, they are (like the 4080 and 4090) in a different price class.

comments.text: This is a good and interesting video. It's interesting to see how the 4070 compares to other GPUs with the same CPU. However, I think it would be equally interesting to see how the performance of the 4070 scales when it's paired with different CPUs. For me, and possibly many others, after having decided to go with the 4070 based on available budget etc, what CPU should I go for to represent a good balanced build where the GPU is not bottlenecked by the CPU? That would, of course, depend on the screen resolution (1080, 2k, 4k). For me right now that would be the most interesting video review, but I've seen very few videos on YouTube that addresses this issue, and I can't find any that are exhaustive enough to answer my question.  For me, it's totally academic and useless to know that the 4090 is almost 3x faster than the 4070 at 4k resolution when using the most super duper CPU. I want to build a balanced system, but I can't afford (or don't want to pay for) a 4090, I don't plan on buying a 4 k monitor for gaming, and I want to spend as little as possible on the CPU.  I'm thinking maybe a 4070 paired with an R5 7600 for 1440 gaming, as that seems like it should be a balanced system, but I'm only guessing and I could be wrong. These are the questions I want answering, and I'm guessing there are lots of other regular people out there who want answers to similar questions. We see lots of videos, including this one, that compares the performances of different GPUs with one specific CPU (in this case an i7-12700KF, or in some cases an i9-13900k, which is again academic and useless information for most people). What about the performance of one specific GPU (in this case the 4070), with different CPUs, or even with older CPUs like 8th, 9th, 10th, or 11th generation Intel CPUs, and equivalent processors from AMD? For example, I've just upgraded my i7-8700k and GTX 1080 ti system, to an i7-8700k with an RTX 4070. The performance has increased a lot and my system now is surprisingly awesome. Most reviews I've seen would suggest pairing an 8700k with a 4070 is total madness, and that I should be put in straight jacket for even having such thoughts, but it works! However, having said that, this is only a temporary upgrade as the i7-8700k is clearly the bottleneck in the system (so you can put that straight jacket back in the closet!). What I want to know, is what CPU would be a sensible upgrade that will make good use of the the 4070 without too much CPU bottleneck? I can't find a single YouTube video that can answer my question. I would like to see a a metric for this, like "CPU bottleneck percentage" for example. That's what I want to see.  Unfortunately, the companies who sponsor these types of videos don't want us to know those things. They just want us to keep upgrading to the latest and greatest, even if it means poor me and you spending money on upgrades that are a total waste of time and money 🙁.

comments.text: I know it wasn't discussed here, but the absolute No. 1 reason I decided to buy the 4070 over the 4060ti -- was the VRAM. I know there are versions of the 4060ti with 16GB of VRAM, but they are expensive. To me, I wanted to future-proof my purchase and that meant I could not get a card with only 8GB of VRAM. comments.text:
Thank you Gamers Nexus for pointing out the value of actual vram, and similarly priced competitors. I just love the inclusion of the 6800 and 6900 series. The price drops actually make them fierce competitors.


Is this card really better than the RTX 3080 12gb? Yes, definitely, but in 2023, it's a hard pass for me. In order for me to consider this card, the MSRP has to be below 500 usd, heck closer to 400usd. The main problem is the lack of vram. We have a mid range level of vram for this card and the price should be treated as such. 1080p games are pushing past 8gb vram in all the newest titles such as RE4, TLOU part 1, Hogwart's Legacy, Dead Space remake, the list goes on and on. at 1440p, the vram usage is around 10 to 11gb vram, but as soon as you turn on RT, it goes over 12 gb. The rx6900xt and rx6950xt from 2 yrs ago is to going to scorch this card in RT at 1440p for upcoming titles. There is no RT advantage moving forward, nobody is going to buy a 600usd card to play at 1080p. (Credit to Daniel Owens for doing vram testing in RE4 remake.)


Watch the  HWUB video comparing the RTX3070 to the RX6800. In 2 yrs time, we're going to see another video comparing this 4070 with the RX6900XT, and the unreleased RX7800xt and we're going to go through all the testing and find the VRAM lacking on the 4070 being the bottleneck for greatness.

In my mind, this is a 4060ti pretending to be a 4070 priced like a 3080. For the love of god, don't fall for this BS marketing and skip this card. Frame Generation isn't real frames, it does nothing for input latency, the whole point of having higher fps is responsiveness with smoothing. You only get visual smoothing with DLSS3.

comments.text:
We're seeing more games now that are really hammering VRAM usage, and I think reviewers will need to update their test suites, which are no longer representative of current or near-future titles.
Hogwarts 4K uses 13 GB VRAM, TLOU 1440p uses over 12 GB VRAM, RE4 + RT 4K uses 14.6 GB VRAM, Godfall 4K uses 12.6 GB VRAM.
This is almost unprecedented, we haven't run out of VRAM since the GTX 970 4GB, or the Voodoo 3 cards of yesteryear. It's also very bad news for last-gen nvidia cards, where RE4 + RT crashes on an 8 GB 3070 Ti, even at 1080p, and embarrassingly, will run on 12 GB 3060 cards.
It is also not a good sign for 4070/Ti users, as 12 GB is now looking like 'not enough' for 1440p and 4K  gaming. If I had bought a 4070 Ti for $900, I'd be pretty miffed at having to turn textures to High or Medium to run current and future games, because nvidia was too cheap to architect a 256-bit AD104 with 16 GB of frame buffer.

comments.text:
I generally don't understand why reviewers never take into account the huge amount of taxes people have to pay on top of these products. For a product to be appealing to consumers, in most places; especially in Europe, the price including tax has to appeal. Here we don't look at 'oh this costs X without tax and Y with tax'. No. There is one price and one price only, and that is the price including tax. 

So this thing in the Netherlands for example where tax is 21%, or Germany 19%, you take whatever Dollar/euro value they used; say 1,10. So 600 / 1,10 * 1,21 is a minimum of 660 or 649 euros! First of all, that is much higher than the number '600', second of all it is in EUROS. This in Dollars converted would be 660 * 1,10  = 726 USD!! And I did not even count the extra mark up they do.

Come on guys, try to take these things in consideration when you are talking about 'value for consumers'. This is a realistic scenario. The cheapest third party model here in NL is 690 euros! Im sure this is the same case for nearly all countries in Europe and perhaps even in other parts of the world and certain states in the US.

For the smart asses who will reply below saying 'u can't take into account every country': no shit Sherlock! That's not what I'm suggesting. There could be a systematic way to show even an artificial value to get retail shelf price feel. Already getting murricans crying in the comments lmao.

The scores from the compare cards I assume are from the date given, meaning using drivers from that date. New AMD drivers will actually give all of these AMD cards anywhere from a 10-20% increase in performance and FPS, if not more in certain cases.
For example, the LTT review was done with new drivers (Linus actually made a note about it as well), and while they didn't include a 6900 or 6950 XT, they found that the 6800 XT consistently and easily beats the 4070. If looking for a card around this price point, and assuming RT isn't some deal-breaker for you (not sure why it would be personally), a Radeon 6800/6900/6850 XT seems the way to go. That or maybe wait for the new 7800 XT which is expected to retail at launch for $650-$900. While you would expect that card to handily beat all these card (except maybe the 6950), I'm seen mixed reports on whether it has 12GB or 16G. Not talking about the power consumption and thermal performance of the 4070 compared to the 3080 and 6950 feels really disingenuous. You spent the whole review comparing a couple percent performance here, a couple percent performance there, praising the old cards, but then when you get to power and thermals, which the 4070 blatantly wins at, you're quiet about it.

My daughter and her husband now use my old system parts...  Ryzen 3 1400, ASRock B350, 16GB memory, GeForce GTX 1060, WD 1GB hard drive, Antec 550w PS, Antec Case, and a 23" 1080p monitor.  I have a Ryzen 5 5600, ASRock B550, 16GB memory, AMD Radeon 6650XT, 1TB NVME gen 3+, 4TB backup drive, ASUS 28" 4k monitor, Creative Labs 5.1 surround speakers, Razor Mamba KB+M, LG Blu-ray burner, Antec case, 1080P web cam, Canon TR4720 printer...  It is a good system.

I can not justify putting more than $100 or so into most parts and $200-300 into a few parts.  The increased quality or performance is just not worth the massive increase in cost.  I got a good 5 years out of my Ryzen 1400.  Heck in the last 10-15 years the only thing I have ever had die was a cheap $50 SSD I got on Black Friday 4-5 years ago.  It only lasted a year. comments.text:
I think this is an okish card, due to inflation, $500 is around $570 so its more like a $30-$20 price increase increase at a price point where that doesnt really make a difference to anybody that could afford it. Its still borderline stagnation since its slightly slower than a 3080, but the realistic price of the 3080 when everything settled was over $800, lets be honest. It also does have an extremely strong feature set and im way more confident in 12gb at 1440p with RT on and 4K in general than i am with 10 for the future, bus size be damned.

The problem is if you dont care about RT, NVENC for live streaming, nvidia broadcast, power draw, reflex or having a good upscaler or frame generation, then the 6950XT for the same price just makes sense for even better performance in raster and 16gb of vram. More so, you can buy a 6800XT for around $500 right now and that will perform relatively the same in raster as this and have the 16gb of vram people feel more comfortable right now with. It will definitely have a worse feature set for sure, but i dont think for most people that worse feature set really matters and theres a lot of fear around not having enough vram right now even though im personally in the camp of 12gb is gonna be enough for 1440p RT for a while and 4K non RT for a while in any game that isnt broken with a memory leak and things like that. Under current economic conditions people a high end 1440p, entry level 4K card for $500 is a big deal, and while i think RDNA3 will continue to be a flop for technical issues and prices, RDNA2 is time test pretty reliable and selling at a reasonable price range when Ampere, Ada and RDNA3 arent. And honestly unless youre gaming at 4K or using RT or productivity, you really dont need more than anything RDNA2 can offer. I still dont think driver wise theyre up to where Nvidia is because they literally arent, but ive had 2 RDNA2 cards and we still have one of them and minus weird uncommon exceptions it runs great on everything. I personally use a 4070 Ti cause it does exactly what i want no more or less, but i have no issues using RDNA2. Im just weird and aesthetically minded enough to notice RT even mid intense gameplay and live stream and do some productivity stuff as a hobby. If it wasnt for that id prob have bought a 6800XT and called it a day.

comments.text: The 6950xt is going to cost a ton more if you figure in electricity cost, but it's also kind of an unfair comparison because the performance is a lot higher, and the card will likely operate at a lower utilization if you target the same performance/fps, and then the math gets complicated. If you want to compare 4070 to the almost identically performing 6800xt, then the difference is much smaller. I ran a quick calculation using average US electricity price and an estimate of 4 hours a day "max power runtime" which should simulate a pretty good upper bound for most people's usage, and the difference is about $18 per year. If you count a typical upgrade frequency of once per 4 years, the life time saving will be about $50 for the 4070. Considering that the current actual MSRP premium is about $150 for it over the 6800xt, it's still a bad deal. It will need to run a $50 deficit to the roughly $550 current listing price of the 6800xt, which means unless the 4070 is selling at or below $500, it remains beaten in value.

comments.text:
The problem with presenting such a number is there are too many variables.  Power costs are all over the map and any sort of attempt to normalize the power consumption and represent a "cost of ownership" would be futile.  But we can calculate a scenario to give you an idea:

Looking at Steve's charts, at full load, the 6950 XT uses 377W and the 4070 uses 203W - that's 174W more for the 6950 XT.  
If you were to run the 6950 XT at 100% for 8 hours, that would be (174W x 8 hours) = 1392 Wh or 1.392 kWh.  
If your electricity costs US$0.10 per kWh (which is the average according to a quick Google search but I suspect it's probably higher), then it costs you (1.392 kWh x $0.10/kWh)=$0.1392 more for the 6950 XT per 8 hours at 100% GPU.

So if you run the 6950 XT at 100% for 8 hours per day for an entire year, at $0.10 per kWh, the 6950 XT would cost you (365 days x 1.392 kWh/day x $0.10/kWh) =  $50.80 more per year vs the 4070.

Lots of assumptions to get to that number, but there ya go.  Hope this helps!

comments.text: It's funny, but blame this horrid GPU market and its total lack of value on - believe it or not - iPhones. comments.text:
​ @zdspider6778  It's just the realities of the market. Prices in an open market are set by what the market will bare. And since the market seems more than happy to pay the price - companies have no incentive to lower pricing. And while you say "but AMD could compete on price and gain market share!" well - historically, any time AMD has done something like this: NVIDIA simply drops a new SKU basically overnight, and the price advantage AMD had evaporates and people continue buying NVIDIA cards.

Now - the next few years should be interesting (we are talking 2-3 generations of cards). First - Intel's Cards should see dramatic improvement given the first generation is decent and has seen dramatic driver improvements since launch. Second - We should start seeing the pay offs of AMD's acquisitions of a few different companies and their technology to improve aspects of their existing products.

In some regards - while in most cases you need 4-5 competitors in a market to see price competition, in GPU's the window of opertunity for competition is basically restricted to Price, and Performance - with AIB's largely dealing with the service side of things. With Intel entering the market and wanting some market share - we are likley to see some price competition start to happen across the product stacks, but don't expect this to have a major impact - as it will take some time for Intel's Drivers and general consumer confidence in their product to disrupt market shares.

@HasanWadih  Hardly. Its quite clear you either 1) couldn't understand what I explained to you, or 2) can't process it due to cognitive dissonance. 

It is completely understandable to see a $200-400 price hike compared to where the cost used to be, especially when you accept that Nvidia wants to retain their "profit margin". See those quotations? 

Let me lay reality out for you.

Since 2015, the USD has seen a cumulative inflation rate of 27%. The cost of TSMC silicon wafers has skyrocketed, this goes up the lower die size you go. 

In 2015, a sale price per wafer from TSCM cost around $6000. By 2020, it cost upwards of $17,000 (5nm). The 4000 series Nvidia cards are using the 5nm die from TSCM. 

In 2022, shipping freight had nearly doubled. By 2023, the cost of shipping freight has gone up over 300%. 60% of all global goods are shipped via freight. 

Take all that, and slap on the additional cost of vram and all the other additional hardware being shoved on modern cards.

This is the HARD, cold, facts. It's not excuses, its literally the crap show we are in now.

I'm not saying you have to like it, I certainly don't like paying more, but this is reality. We have to go off objective information, do you agree?

Have I proved my point?

comments.text: @JBrinx18  Your PC will only take as much as it needs, which in your case is ~700 watts.  You're reaching the max your 750 watt PSU can handle efficiently.  It's nice to have a bit more headroom for times when transient spikes happen.  The UPS will only pass what is required, so even if you have a larger power supply, the load will stay the same.  You'll just have less stress on the power supply if you size it up a bit.  You'll probably get by fine as is, but there could be  a possibility of a shorter lifespan for the power supply if running it close to it's max rating.

comments.text: @JBrinx18  You would just cause an overload condition on the UPS if you exceed the rating of the UPS.  Short term, it's not usually a problem. You could always get a smaller UPS for your monitor and keep the main one just for the PC alone.

@p0k314COM  RAMlets never learn, so you won't get it, but regardless of that: How much VRAM a GPU has becomes very relevant if you run out of VRAM - and you will if you try to run one a newer poorly optimized game on higher settings. It doesn't matter if you have 8 or 12 or 16 GB VRAM if the game you're running consumes 4 at the settings you want to play at, but it does matter a whole lot of you have 8 and the game needs 12.

The amount of VRAM on a GPU has at a given price point has been something I've put more weight on than pure compute performance since I upgraded from a Radeon 7850 with 2 GB RAM to a RX 570 with 8 GB RAM purely because I was running out of VRAM on the 7850. It matters, and it matters a lot because you can't upgrade the amount of VRAM on a GPU. If your computer as 8 GB RAM and you need more then you've got the option of spending about the same amount you paid for those 8 GB on a 64 GB kit today and you're fine. If you run out of GPU VRAM then you'll have to go buy a whole new GPU, you can't just buy more VRAM and slap it on.

Succinctly put, off the top of your head, try to identify the lowest and highest acceptable price and average out 10+ sold listings within the middle of an estimated bell curve.
